extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, editorial office staff, and peer-review stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for journals and publishers about how to treat submission volumes, screen manuscripts, and require pre-submission checks and integrity signals to improve peer-review efficiency and research quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of submission volume as a performance indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The total number of submissions a journal receives each year has long ceased to be a useful performance indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat rising submission counts as an unqualified sign of success; chasing ever-more submissions can be deleterious to the industry by increasing volume of low-quality or fraudulent work and masking true journal health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for peer-review costs per submission stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Every submission imposes costs across stages: editorial office checks, desk rejection, peer review management, and production for accepted articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic cost accounting (author gives example: desk rejects ~$20, peer-review rejects ~$100, accepted ~$250) to understand the financial burden of increased submissions and how costs may be redistributed to APCs/subscriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incentives that prioritize submission volume over quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Incentives that reward submission volume lead publishers to welcome more manuscripts even if they are low-quality, increasing editorial burden and downstream costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design KPIs and business models to avoid rewarding raw submission counts; be wary of publication cascades that keep low-quality manuscripts within a publisher’s portfolio purely to recoup editorial costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prequalification of authors prior to submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Require authors to demonstrate they care about doing good science before letting them submit (a prequalification step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors to complete certain improvement or compliance tasks (e.g., data sharing, required checks) before submission; this filters out authors unwilling to meet basic quality expectations and raises the baseline quality of submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pre-submission automated checks and tooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide automated, author-facing checks that assess manuscripts against submission requirements and surface issues before authors submit (examples: blueberg.ai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks can be informational (suggest fixes) or enforced; surfacing missing figures, formatting problems, or policy noncompliance pre-submission saves editorial office time and reduces avoidable desk rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Honest signals' of research integrity required pre-submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Require time-consuming, demonstrable actions that signal research integrity prior to submission, such as sharing data and code, including RRIDs for reagents, and using ORCIDs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Itemize the exact datasets and actions expected; this both communicates the journal’s integrity priorities and holds authors accountable, deterring submissions from those unwilling to comply (including potentially fabricated work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect negative-integrity detection tools from public test-runs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow authors to 'test run' tools that detect negative signals (e.g., image manipulation, paper-mill signatures), because that would let bad actors adapt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep detection methods and access controlled; offer remediation and guidance for honest compliance checks but avoid exposing the mechanics of negative-detection systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reintroduce constructive friction to deter low-quality submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, burdensome initial formatting requirements discouraged low-commitment submissions; modern equivalents (targeted prechecks) can serve the same filter function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat some pre-submission friction as a feature: reasonable time costs (e.g., fixing missing figures or meeting integrity requirements) will deter authors unlikely to meet publication standards while encouraging committed authors to comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider submission fees cautiously as a deterrent
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission fees can deter frivolous submissions but are unpopular and have equity/DEI implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh financial deterrence against the risk of excluding legitimate authors and creating barriers for under-resourced researchers; consider alternatives or waivers to manage fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automate desk assessment and consider auto-reject for clear low-quality submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use automation to triage submissions and potentially auto-reject those that clearly fail basic checks to control editorial workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automation can speed processing and cut costs, but must be used carefully to avoid false positives and unintended exclusion of valid work; transparency about what is checked can help authors comply without exposing detection methods to fraudsters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional pre-vetting of submissions as a possible model
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore shifting some integrity and quality checks upstream to institutions (e.g., institutional tools/subscriptions like PubShield) rather than leaving all burden to journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional pre-vetting could reduce volume pressure on journals, but requires coordination, infrastructure, and institutional commitment; consider pilot collaborations with institutions or shared services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specific, checkable Data Availability Statements (DAS)
rubrics_metrics.description: For sensitive or unavailable data, require D.A.S. that explains why data are not public and how they can be accessed (e.g., contacting authors, institutional group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Itemize expectations for datasets and repositories; actively check compliance rather than accepting broad statements, recognizing that verifying data availability and anonymization is nontrivial and may require EO work or specialist review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance screening measures with DEI and author-experience concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Stronger screening can deter both low- and high-quality authors and have DEI implications by introducing barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pre-submission checks and requirements to minimize unnecessary friction for legitimate authors and provide clear guidance, support, or exemptions where appropriate to protect equity and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform assessment incentives upstream (DORA, CoARA, TARA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address root causes of volume pressure by changing how institutions and funders assess research and researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and operationalize principles from DORA, CoARA, and tools like TARA to reduce publish-or-perish incentives that drive high submission volumes and encourage questionable practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use automation to flag risks while protecting detection methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy AI/tools to flag likely problems and suggest fixes, but avoid revealing detection heuristics that would enable gaming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide actionable feedback to authors (e.g., missing figure) while withholding details that could let bad actors evade integrity checks; combine automated flags with human oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve reviewer/editor experience by raising submission quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher baseline submission quality makes it easier to find willing reviewers and maintain editor enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prequalification and integrity requirements increase the proportion of manuscripts that meet standards on first submission, reducing reviewer fatigue and editorial churn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Itemize required dataset actions to increase compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than vague pleas to 'share your data', require a concise list of the individual datasets and specific repository expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete itemization reduces ambiguity and makes it harder to ignore data-sharing requirements; it also facilitates downstream checks and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat citation- and submission-based metrics with nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics like high citation counts or growing submission numbers can be manufactured or gamed (e.g., citation cartels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on raw metrics as evidence of quality; investigate suspicious patterns and develop more robust, context-aware indicators of journal and article quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigilance against bad-actor behaviors (paper mills, authorships for sale, citation cartels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively identify and call out fraudulent behaviors and systemic gaming that degrade publication quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop policies and tools to detect and exclude paper-mill output, shoddy authorship practices, and citation manipulation; encourage cross-publisher collaboration to share intelligence on bad actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain peer-review anonymity while enabling integrity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-blind review processes may withhold D.A.S. or integrity signals from reviewers to preserve anonymity, complicating data/code verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design workflows that allow editorial checks of integrity without compromising reviewer blinding—e.g., editors or specialist integrity reviewers perform checks while keeping statements hidden from peer reviewers when necessary.
